utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, September 22nd, 2009, and I greet Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I also greet the Defence counsels, all members of the OTP, in great numbers today, and I also greet everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar. I believe he has some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted their lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Josip Jurcevic. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC1042. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit IC1043. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC1044, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC1045. The Prosecution has also submitted its objections to the lists of documents tendered by 3D and 4D via Witness Slobodan Praljak. These lists shall be given Exhibit IC1046 and 1047 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. The Trial Chamber is now going to issue an oral decision, and I will read it slowly. Oral decision on the parties' dead-line to respond to the Rule 92 bis Praljak Defence motion. On September 22nd, 2009, the Prosecution filed, confidentially, a reply to the -- a response to the motion on the admission of Rule 92 bis, motion filed by the Praljak Defence on September 14th regarding the admission of these written statements. The Prosecution is asking mainly for the Praljak motion to be dismissed. Alternatively, the Prosecution is asking for the response dead-line to be extended to November 23rd, 2009. The Trial Chamber believes that it is in the interests of justice to analyse the Praljak Defence motion in light of all replies provided by all parties who wish to reply before ruling on the admission. However, the Trial Chamber believes that the extension of the dead-line requested by the Prosecution would significantly delay the procedure. Consequently, the Trial Chamber extends the dead-line for all parties wishing to respond to the Praljak motion until October 28, 2009. There, in a word, in a nutshell, all parties have until October 28, a month from now, to file their submissions in response to the Praljak Defence motion. I believe everyone understood this oral decision. Now, as far as the schedule is concerned, we've been informed by a letter by Mr. Kovacic that the witness Skender could only come on Thursday. Is that it, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, exactly. [Interpretation] Mr. Skender will be coming in as planned. As I said, we tried to speed the schedule up, but he wasn't able to fly in, and he's coming in from Corsica this evening, so we won't be able to see him before tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, the first witness, Arbutina Alojz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning [as interpreted], sir. Could you please tell us your name, sir, name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alojz Arbutina. The 24th of November, 1931. I was born in France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were born in France. Where were you born in France, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Haltbont [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must be retired, given your age. Could you tell us what your last occupation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a skilled electrician working in the company Elektra, and I've been retired since 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in court or is this the first time that you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time, here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Let me give you some information so that this hearing runs smoothly and for the best for everyone. First, you will be answering questions which will be put to you by the Praljak Defence. You might even answer questions put to you by General Praljak, himself, if those questions are within his competence. Then after that phase -- normally, this should take about an hour, so after this hour, the other counsels for the other accused who are in front of you, on your left, will also be putting questions to you, and this phase should last about 30 minutes for all other accused. The Prosecution had an hour for his questions, but he told us last week that he did not intend to ask any questions, after all. The four Judges on the Bench might ask you a few questions. They probably will, actually, questions on the elements that you will be giving in your answers. Please try and be concise in your answers. If you do not understand a question, don't hesitate to ask the one putting the question to you to reformulate it. If at any point in time you feel ill at ease or unwell - you never know because a hearing is always stressful and can sometimes be very uncomfortable - so just raise your hand so we can just break for a while. I don't think that this is much of a surprise for you. I'm sure that Mr. Praljak's counsels have told you all about this hearing, and since you -- I also want to tell you that since you're talking the same language as Mr. Praljak's counsel, wait for them to be finished with their question before you answer, to make sure that the both of you don't overlap. Thank you. You have the floor, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to you all and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon, Mr. Arbutina. I'm over here. You can look at me. I'm over here. You can turn towards me. Well, you can look where you like, but just I want you to know that I'm asking you the questions from here. I can see that the Prosecutor glanced at the papers that you have in front of you. What is it that you have there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Well, I have the statements that I gave earlier on in Croatia, in Sunja, and I have that before me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You said that you gave a statement. Did you give that statement of your own free will and to the best of your recollections and knowledge, and did you say what you said truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did make a truthful statement of my own free will, without anybody having to persuade me to do so, and I am happy to be a witness for the general.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were born in France, but where do you live?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I live in Sunja, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, that is additional information because we don't have your date of birth or address in the statement, so that's why I asked you that. And since when have you lived in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Since 1936, when we settled there, my parents and I, and that was the Yugoslavia of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what the situation was like in Sunja up until the beginning of the war in the Republic of Croatia, or, rather, until the beginning of the war in Sunja and when that war actually broke out?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: The population of Sunja was mixed. There were more Croats than other -- than the Serbs. And in Sunja, itself, the war began on the 27th of July, 1991, in the morning, between 7.00 and 8.00, with a mortar attack. This was a great shock to us. It came as a big surprise, because on the 26th, for example, the 26th of July, that is, I had a friend - he was a Serb - and the day before the attack I was with them -- with him, but on the day of the attack, they were no longer in Sunja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did they inform you about that; that is to say, did they tell you there would be an attack? Did they know there would be an attack?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: They didn't inform me about anything, and there were even cases where there were very close relations of kinship and kumship, and they didn't inform me about anything, they just disappeared. So there were cases like that just a few days before the attack and, actually, on the 26th, or between the 26th and 27th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 12 of the Croatian text, you say that they left across the railway line. What does that mean; that the local Serbs went across the railway line or what?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Well, that's what we called the border. In fact, the railway line was the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The border of what?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: The border between us and the paramilitary forces there, Martic's men, the Chetniks, and the inhabitants who were in Serb villages across the railway line, beyond the railway line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that is, otherwise, the territory of the Republic of Croatia; right? It's not the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina? It was the separation line between two sides, that kind of border; right?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: No -- well, yes, it's an area of Croatia. It was our local border, so to speak, and we knew that across the way, across the railway line, you couldn't go any further, you couldn't go to that side, because when the actual attack began in the morning, we organised ourselves straight away, and during the day and during the night the civilian population was evacuated, both Croats and the Serbs who had stayed on, or they were near the railway station and were, therefore, under threat. They were under threat from the attacks that they started to launch against us, so those people were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, how was the line organised? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I think I'll be able to describe this to the Trial Chamber. The line, the boundary, was the railway line, and from the railway line to Sisak and the road running to Sisak --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I apologise, but the question was whether the line was well organised, well set up, well fortified, or were there any problems? I'm not asking you where it was, but what it was like there on the first day, the second day, at the beginning of all this.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to describe it. At the beginning, just to be on the safe side, we were sort of on a peninsula. The River Sava was an exit for us if the place were to fall, but we couldn't go to the left or the right because the line was from the Sava River towards the station, and part of that station, and then down Vladimir Masal Street, the villages of Krimadze [phoen], Metbogovac [phoen], and across the fields and meadows.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Were there any bunkers, were there any trenches, any obstacles? Were the soldiers well protected, any barriers put up, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: At the beginning, we didn't have anything because we weren't expecting anything like that. The only thing -- the only barriers we had was up at the station, where there was the station depot warehouse, and at first, up at the front-line, as we referred to it, the railway line, the front-line, there was the police. Well, we called it the militia first, but then it was called the police. And there was a few volunteers who were organised at that first stage, during those first days, until the 2nd Guards Company arrived, and the reserve police force, I think, arrived on the third day from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, was that the situation at the front-line throughout or were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: In September -- well, the first commander was Zarko Pesa, and so in September General Praljak arrived. And when he took over the command in Sunja, the situation was quite different. But, nevertheless, it was a difficult situation, difficult to deal with all those volunteers. They didn't actually understand what was going on. They didn't realise that it was a war. And when General Praljak arrived, then they began to organise the front-lines better, their bunkers were built, trenches, barriers, and all the rest of it, and the discipline improved at that time, too. Everything became better organised. How can I explain this? Well, us locals, it was difficult when a local person was a commander and so on, and I was an officer in the previous army. I had a rank, I was lieutenant, and I -- when I told the young guys that we had to build bunkers and so on, they wouldn't really listen. It was all sporadic. But when General Praljak arrived, then discipline was raised to a much higher level and there was a certain measure of respect, because he was somebody from other parts, he wasn't a local, because if locals tend to issue orders to locals, that's a different matter, but everybody felt they knew how to defend the area themselves. But when Praljak came in, that was quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're telling us that General Praljak arrived -- you were born in 1931, so in 1992 you were over 60. When you saw General Praljak coming, what did you think at the time? Did you think -- was he being sent by Zagreb or is he just coming just like Zorro, you know, coming to the rescue?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer your question. He came as a volunteer, of his own will. He was brought by Zarko Pesa, who was our previous commander. He came of his own will. He came to Sunja to help us, to assist us in defending us from our enemy that was across the railway line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are telling us that Zarko Pesa asked him to come, and he came as a volunteer. So could you tell us why it is that someone who came from the outside is suddenly commanding the troops, whereas on the field there are people like you? You had been a lieutenant in the JNA, so why is it that it was a person coming from the outside that ended up commanding the troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this did not come from the outside, that this came from the Main Staff of the Republic of Croatia for the defence of Croatia, but he came as a volunteer. He came to help us, and he made sure that we were more active in everything. I don't know how to answer. And as I told you, it was easier for somebody who came from the outside than from a local midst, because that person commands more respect, because I, as a local, if I wanted to tell you something or explain something to you because I had some military knowledge and experience, I could go on talking and asking people to do this or that or the other, but then the response would always be, Don't you tell us what we should do. We know very well how we should do it. I don't know if there is anything else I can tell you in answer to your question. There were people who made bunkers on their sheds near their homes or behind the sheds. Of course, people had cattle and manure was behind the shed, and behind that was a cornfield, and of course that he could see, if somebody was walking through the cornfield, he was visible at a 30-metre distance. He could not come closer -- any closer to the shed because there was a clear field of vision. I would explain to them that the enemy could crawl through the cornfields and throw a hand-grenade on them, or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Arbutina, in the month of July 1991, did you know anything about the organisation of the Croatian Army? Did you know what was in place at the time? Was there any organisation in place, were there any brigades in place, or was this developed gradually after that? I'm talking about the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: In Croatia, there were things, and I'm talking about my area. At that time, we started organising ourselves. First of all, we had volunteers, and then, on the 1st of September, I believe, there were first mobilisation papers distributed. And before the 20th of July, we were all volunteers, as part of a unit that was organised together with people from Sisak. We were a company in Sunja, and that company grew with time. More people joined, and that's how we became a brigade, and then we became a home guard regiment. And there were also active brigades, but our brigade was a reserve brigade. In Sunja, we were assisted by a guards brigade and some other units from other brigades, from the 102nd and 101st Brigades, and all those things changed before 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just waiting for the record to be finished. Mr. Arbutina, when we were talking about the arrival of General Praljak, when did that happen, when did he arrive in Sunja? When did he first arrive in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: In the month of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any contacts with the general while he was in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At the very beginning, I was appointed by the Crisis Staff as the commander of the logistics there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about the attitude of General Praljak towards the civilians? Do you know anything about that? How did he treat the civilians who remained living in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I can say that General Praljak did not make any difference between the civilians and the troops. He looked after everybody equally. I was appointed the assistant commander for logistics, and, as such, I cooperated very strictly with the general, and we discussed everything that concerned my position as a logistics man. Every evening, we had a short briefing. Every evening, I was supposed to go to him, because by then we received all the food from Sisak, and that's why I had to go to Sisak every day, to fetch the food. And after that, I always had to go and seek the general's signature. And then once I asked him, General, sir, I don't think that I should come to you every evening just for the signature. You know that I have to go, but you don't have to know that I am going to fetch 300 kilos of potato or 100 kilo of onion. And he said, Well, I don't see a problem. This will be one less worry for me if you don't come for my signature. And from then on, things changed. However, our co-operation was very good, and whatever I needed, whatever assistance I may have needed, if there was a problem, whenever I addressed the general, there was always good co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Were people hungry in Sunja? Was there enough food?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: There was enough food because we looked after that. The general's order personally to me was that there shouldn't be any shortages, not only for the troops but also for the civilians. There were a lot of Croatian civilians as well as Serbs who remained living in the area. Later on, they joined the Croatian Army. And we also had a few Muslims who lived in Sunja. But he would often tell me, Please make sure that everybody has enough to eat, all the civilians. And we even have some elderly Serbs that we took care of, and they all regularly received food and provisions, just like the troops. There were no shops where one could get food. The situation was not normal. There were shops, but they were closed down. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Serbian civilians, did they remain living in Sunja of their own will? Were they incarcerated? Did they lead a normal life? What can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: They led a normal life. There were no differences between them and the rest of the population, the Croatian population. For example, we treated everybody equally. Maybe there were -- there was some sporadic taunting, but that was really sporadic and insignificant; that they stayed of their own will. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I have to say that the neighbourhood from the railway station to the center of Sunja, half of that part may be 500 or 600 metres away from the railway station, we removed from that area both Croats and Serbs, and there were Serbs who remained in Sunja as well as the others who were further away from that area, and the rest left across the River Sava and joined their relatives in Sisak or Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you chase them away or did they leave of their own will, those that left? And I mean the Serbs that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I know what you're saying. Nobody chased them away. Those who wanted to leave left. Because some order had been introduced into the command of the company in our firefighters hall, that's where the command was, and then when Pesa was there, they had the Main Staff, and when Mr. Praljak came. However, initially before they came, those who wanted to leave, they would be given passes for the barge to get across the river to the other parts of Croatia where they had relatives. There was no expulsion or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I have two more questions for you, sir. The first question is: What was the treatment of soldiers, and do you know anything about the discipline among the troops?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I can only say that discipline improved significantly after General Praljak arrived. He told them, We are a military and we are defending our homeland, and we have to abide by military rules, and we have to discharge our military duties in a proper way. It was very difficult to introduce order and discipline. However, the general was not very rigid in his behaviour, but he asked for discipline and order. And what I found very impressive was, for example, our morning briefings. General Praljak introduced a flag-raising ceremony every morning, and every morning the anthem was played by a soldier, and then we had very short briefings. Mr. Praljak would then say, The 1st Company, any problems, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th, Logistics? And those briefings were very short, not more than half an hour, and then he would say to us, Let's go on, lads, let's continue working and making sure we know what we are doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When did General Praljak leave Sunja? Do you know the date or just an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I believe that it was in [indiscernible] 1992, in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the Defence is concerned, we have no more questions. I would just like Mr. Arbutina's statement under 3D03699 to be tended into evidence. I don't know if General Praljak believes that there is something to be added to my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, I have a whole series of follow-up questions to put to you. I'd like to get back to the question of the civilians. Sunja was part of a municipality, and if I've understood you correctly, this small settlement had, by and large, 1.300 inhabitants when the census was conducted in 2001. So in 1991/1992, one could reasonably presume that there were at least a thousand inhabitants. The 2001 census indicates that 17 per cent of these people were Serbs. Ten years prior to that, if we calculate on the basis of a thousand inhabitants, there were approximately 100 Serbs, 40 to 45 families, all in all, according to my calculations. You told us that there was a street on the other side of this station, and you said that the Croats and the Serbs left from that particular point. You decided that, but you remained very discreet as far as the fate of the Serbs was concerned. Why did you ask the Serbs living on that street to leave? When I mean you, I don't mean you, personally. I mean the Croats in general. Why did you ask them to leave their houses, their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody persuaded them to leave or forced them to leave. You said that our place was small. Yes, it was. Before the war, Sunja was part of Sisak municipality. We were just a local commune. And to make things clearer to you, I have to say that this part or this neighbourhood between the railway line and the Sava River was occupied by Croats; 90 per cent were Croats. Sunja, Krivaj, Zremen, Bobovac, Gornja and Donja Letina, and the border on the Sava River. Across the railway line, there were villages with a predominantly Serb population. We called that area Maksimir, but there were also Citvertkovac [phoen], Drljaca, Donji Hrastovac, Paukova [phoen], Mala and Velika Gradusa. Those villages were part of the locale commune of Sunja, but all those villages were inhabited by the Serbian population. And I stated in my statement that the part between the railway line and the Sava River and the streets in that area, that's where the Socialist Alliance was located. And along the Sinjak [phoen]-Sunja-Dubica road and where the road forks off from Hrastovac to Hrvatska Kostajnica, in that part we could not even go to Voldera [phoen] Polje, where there was local population between the railway line leading to Novska. We were on the very outskirt of the streets called Vladimir Nazer [phoen] and Milos Podric [phoen], and those two streets led towards the railway line leading to Sisak. We had only the area where the Vajda company, and that's very close to the railway station, maybe 50 or 60 metres away from the railway station, but we could not enter Vajda, we could not go to Vajda because of them, and that part was what we called -- and it was our front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interrupting you because you haven't answered my question. What I would like to know is what became of the civilians. Did they leave of their own accord or did you force them to leave? What happened to them? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody forced them to leave. I have to -- if I may, I would like to finish my sentence. They left of their own will, without us even knowing when they left. On the 27th, there were no longer there. Those who remained there were just there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the 27th of what month? You said on the 27th, they weren't there anymore. Which months do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th of July, 1991. And if I might be allowed to just add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't allow you because my time is invaluable. On the 27th of July, 1991, had they all left or did some remain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my statement I said that some of them stayed. Those who stayed, well, there were no repercussions that they were exposed to. They went where they wanted in Croatia, where they had relatives and so on, of their own free will, and the younger members joined the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many Serbs remained in Sunja, how many exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't give you any figures, but in the Croatian Army there were more than ten, and three Muslims, and they were inhabitants of Sunja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that some Serbs and Muslims joined the Croatian Army. What I'm interested in: How many Serb civilians remained in their houses in Sunja; one, ten, fifty? How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About a dozen, ten or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us that General Praljak asked you to look after logistical affairs. These Serbs who were there, did they have enough to eat, did they have enough food, like all the others, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all had the same food, just like the Croatian Army; not only the Serb inhabitants at the beginning, but the Croats too, all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understood, in Sunja there must have been fighting. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were major battles to begin with, but they didn't manage to break through our front-lines, but they did shell us heavily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Among the people living in Sunja, because of the shelling, were any of the people killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about four. Two women -- or, rather, three women were killed in the shelling, and one man. I'm referring to the civilians now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Sunja forces headed by General Praljak, did you capture any enemies or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While General Praljak was the commander, we didn't have any prisoners, but at the beginning, the very beginning, we had two, one before General Praljak was the commander, while Zarko Pesa was the commander, that is, and we exchanged one of them for one of ours, one of our soldiers who was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of my last questions. Now, as far as you remember, General Praljak exercised command for how long, and when was he no longer a commander in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said in September 1991. I'm not sure of the exact date when he took over. And in April, he left Sunja, so that was the period of time that he was commander there, commander of the defence of Sunja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. You told us a while ago that every morning General Praljak hoisted the flag and someone was playing the trumpet. I assume this was the Croatian national anthem which was being played. General Praljak then held a briefing session which lasted approximately 30 minutes, as you told us, and then he questioned everybody to understand what was going on. What you have described to us, did it apply to the period of time, i.e., six months that General Praljak was there, i.e., hoisting the flag, briefing? Did this occur every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every day, every day while he was the commander there. And when he left Sunja, the tradition continued. Well, I can't say "tradition," actually, but, anyway, this continued in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the troops were concerned, how many men accounted for the forces in Sunja; 100, 200, 400? How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first couple of months, the forces in Sunja, and not only there, but depending on the period, it was between 1500 and 2.000 soldiers, 2.500, and from other regiments, special units and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranging from 1.500 to 2.000 men, which is quite a substantial figure. In any army, you always have black sheep, people who start drinking, who start fighting, who start looting and pilfering. As far as you know, were these soldiers prosecuted in any way? Were any disciplinary measures taken against these people? Did General Praljak hold a very strict position vis-a-vis these men who had violated the discipline in the army or was it total chaos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- well, just like you said, Your Honour, at times somebody drank more than they should, but I think discipline was at a high level, generally speaking. There wasn't any major chaos because we were all together at the time. We didn't look at each other's ethnicity. We were just all there together, defending our thresholds. And if I might be allowed to say, well, I'd like to mention to the Trial Chamber that Sunja, and we called it breakfast, lunch, and supper, whenever we would distribute food to the soldiers, there was shelling, non-stop, until UNPROFOR arrived in April, and then the shelling was not as fierce as it had been before that. But on a daily basis, it was between 100, 200, and 300 shells falling on Sunja. But when UNPROFOR came, over 40.000 shells were dropped on Sunja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the presence of General Praljak, did you attend any briefing sessions which aimed at setting up the defence of that locality, and do you remember what kind of instructions General Praljak may have given the soldiers? You were a lieutenant in the JNA. Therefore, the question I am putting to you is this: Were the forces in Sunja commanded by someone who was in the know or did General Praljak give the impression that he was an amateur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At every briefing session while the commander was Praljak, and also the other commanders too, I was present, and I had the rank of major, major of the Croatian Army. It was like an assistant commander for logistics, let's say. And every day, I had contacts and cooperated with General Praljak because the briefings were in the morning, and then I had my duties to attend to. I had to go to the 1st Logistics Base which was in Sisak, and then it was expanded to Zagreb. So I had to travel around to procure goods, weapons, and everything else. And I'd just like to say that at the beginning, we weren't armed at all, not so much at all. The weapons that we had, well, at the beginning you had the various hunters with their hunting rifles, and I said that. I said, in response to a question from Defence counsel, until the 2nd Guards Company and reserve police from Zagreb arrived, they helped us a great deal because they were well armed, so then we were -- we were less afraid than we were at the beginning when we only had the hunting rifles. And at the beginning, we had to secure all access roads with anti-tank barriers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. As you can imagine, I could continue for hours. This is now my last question. You told us that you were assistant commander in charge of logistical affairs. As far as you remember, did General Praljak sign the military orders or didn't he sign much and he had devolved this to his assistants, or did he want to check everything out, read everything, and sign everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I understood your question, I can say that there were no written orders because we agreed about everything at the briefings. And at the beginning, and I'm speaking about myself as the logistics man, I needed his signature from time to time. And when I said that, he stopped doing this, he gave me the assignments, and then I took care about those things. The only thing was that I was to report to him orally, tell him what I had done. And if I had any -- encountered any problems, I would ask him for help, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought General Praljak wanted to put a few questions to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Arbutina.

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think I referred to you and called you Monsieur Arbutina, given the fact that you were born in France; right?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, now, any family -- older family, Croatian, Serb, or Muslim, were they ever left -- allowed to go hungry without you being given orders to see that they were fed?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was winter-time; right? What about fuel for heating? Is it true that all the elderly and families where there were elderly persons, that they were given the means for heating free of charge? Did I give you orders to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: Yes. We took great care about that, great care about the poor and the elderly. We supplied them with fuel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was a single house set fire to in Sunja while I was there?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was any house looted while I was there, broken into?

utterances.speaker: ALOJZ ARBUTINA
utterances.text: No. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Arbutina, for coming here. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask the other Defence counsels what they intend to do. Ms. Nozica, Mr. Khan, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas. Well, he's not with us, but what about the Prlic Defence? Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Dr. Prlic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Petkovic Defence has no questions, either, for this witness. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The Coric Defence has no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, I believe you had no questions. Do you have any?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Arbutina, your testimony is now over. Most questions were asked by the Praljak Defence, and I also put a few questions to you, as well as General Praljak. The other parties and the Prosecution have decided that they would not ask you any questions. Thank you for coming to testify for General Praljak. I wish you a safe return home, and I will now ask our Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is already here. They arrived at the same time. I mean the next witness, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I believe we will have a break right now, and then we will resume with the new witness after this 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding Witness Miroslav Crnkovic, I believe I understood that you need an hour, Mr. Kovacic. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we have saved some time with the previous witness, my learned friend Ms. Pinter is going to examine the next witness, and it may take a bit longer than just an hour. In any case, our plan is for her to try and finish with this witness by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope the translation is working correctly. Could you please give us your name, surname, and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Crnkovic, 24th November 1969, Hrvatska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your job at the moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a retired officer of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite young to be retired. Could you tell us what was your rank when you left the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in court regarding the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Let me give you some information on the way this hearing is going to unfold. Ms. Pinter is going to put questions to you. She must have already explained to you that she was going to ask you a number of questions. You will answer these questions. After that, the counsels of the other accused might decide to put questions to you, and the Prosecutor, who is on your right, might also decide to cross-examine you and put questions to you. And the Judges on this Bench might -- actually will put questions to you. So please try to be very specific in your answers, because time is of the essence, and I'm sure that as a former officer of the Croatian Army, you know what this means, that time is of the essence. You know exactly how to be specific in your answers. If you don't understand a question, which can happen, please ask the person putting the question to reformulate it. We have breaks every hour and a half. The next break will be in an hour and 25 minutes. But if for some reason you feel unwell, just raise your hand and say that you need a break so you can rest, even if we have to bring a physician or something, but this is a possibility. I wanted to tell you all this to put you at ease. It's true that testifying is an ordeal, you know, and you'll remember it all throughout -- for your entire life, I'm sure, so it's best to make sure that everything runs smoothly. I'll now give the floor to Ms. Pinter, and she will put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Crnkovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You've been provided instructions from the Trial Chamber. The only thing I need to repeat is not to speak too fast and wait for my question to be over before you start providing your answer, and the same thing applies to me. I will also have to make sure that we do not overlap. Before you, you should have a summary under number 3D03758 that has already been provided to our learned friends in the OTP and the Trial Chamber. Have you read this summary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Does this summary contain something that you didn't say or that has been mis-recorded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, as regards His Honour Antonetti's words, I'm going to ask you: How come you retired? He was surprised to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the circumstances. I was seriously injured during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you are an invalid?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have provided His Honour Judge Antonetti with your personal details, and could you please also tell us something about your work path, i.e., where you were, what unit were you a member of, and where you served during the war between 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: From the month of March 1991 up to the month of June 1991, I was a member of the Special Police of the Croatian Army. From the month of June 1991 to the moment when I was wounded and pensioned off eventually, I was a member of the 2nd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later. Could you please tell us where you served as a member of the Croatian Army, in which territories?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were mostly territories around my place of residence. I'm talking about Banovina and, more specifically, the towns of Glina, Kozibrod, Sunja -- not Kosovo, Kozibrod, Sunja, and after that for some ten days I was in Mostar, and four or five days before I was wounded I was in Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will start with Sunja. However, you have just mentioned the fact that you were in the theatre of war of Banovina. What is Banovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Banovina is the area around Cerska comprising Sunja, Glina, Kozibrod, Hrvatska, Kostajnica. That's the area I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Sunja on the 31st of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the front-line as it was when you arrived in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: The front-line, as such, did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: We found houses, some sandbags on the windows which were supposed to serve as protection and serve as a defence line. However, that could not function in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you say "when we arrived," who do you mean? Which unit arrived there, which brigade? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about my company, a company of the 2nd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: How many men were there in the company?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Forty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The front-line, as you found it when you arrived in Sunja, did it remain that way throughout your stay in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. It was extended from the front-line to the second line to the third line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: All that happened after General Praljak's arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation and the changes in the front-line? Were the lines reinforced, were the trenches dug, were the bunkers built? What was the front-line composition?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: When General Praljak arrived, he saw what the situation was, and he embarked on the process to reinforce the line. He established civilian protection, composed of men who did not carry arms at the moment, and he turned them into auxiliary work platoons that were in charge of supplying the front-line with sandbags, logs that were all used to build bunkers. He met with resistance. I was also among those who did not like all that, because we were all very tired, and he started digging, himself. When we saw that we didn't have a choice and we joined him. A few days after the bunker was dug between the railway station where we were billeted, there was an attack during which the whole railway station was set ablaze and destroyed. I can simply say that the bunker that was dug and all the other bunkers saved our lines. That's how the second line was established, the third line was established, the fourth as well. All the men, all the soldiers who resided in the villages, were organised at the highest possible level. Everybody knew what they were supposed to do, what their tasks were. And to put it simply, everything functioned really excellently at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you remember, as you sit today, how many bunkers were constructed in that way, how many trenches?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, over 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the work platoon. Can you tell me whether that work platoon went to the front-line on its own to dig bunkers and trenches? Did they have some sort of security? Were they exposed to enemy attacks? Did somebody go with them? Were they guarded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: We provided security for them. And when I say "we," we were the unit that was active on the front-line. We were in front of them, and in any case of a possible attack we would inform them and alert them to that. So they were safe as much as one could be safe in a war. In any case, I don't remember that any civilian got hurt when reinforcing the front-line or digging bunkers or trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you say "civilians," we're talking about younger people, or middle-aged people, or elderly people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Middle-aged people who at that moment were not assigned to any military units because there was not enough weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You were in different theaters of war. Could you please tell us something about discipline in Sunja? How was it established, and what did discipline mean for Sunja? Can you give us some examples of that, discipline among soldiers, discipline of soldiers, vis-a-vis others, particularly civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Before General Praljak arrived, there was no discipline to speak of. He opposed any attempts to breach discipline. He did not allow any departures from the normal military norm. He did not allow anybody to loot property, to set anybody's property to fire, to loot property from abandoned houses. All the houses were abandoned. And if -- one can say that there were all sorts of people, and some of them, you had to engage in physical fights with some of them in order to curb their behaviour. I can give you some examples. I can mention three of my soldiers who dis-appropriated from a house five plates, five spoons, some three knives, and a small black-and-white TV, and one of the members of my unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You don't have to mention their names if --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the members of my unit lost his house because it had been burned by the enemy. His wife had called him and told him that there was nothing in the apartment where she was moved to in Sisak. The same three or four soldiers were caught on the barge as they were crossing the river to go to Sisak, and they were returned to Sunja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who caught them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: A member of the police caught them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was it civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the military police did not exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, one of my friends, who was coming back from the command, from headquarters, told me, since I was up at the front-line, that General Praljak had disarmed them, stripped them of their insignia and badges, and lined them up in front of the fire brigade in Sunja, which was a place that served as a headquarters for the home guards, of sorts. And at that point in time, I got into my car, went down there, asked him what was going on. He said that, quite simply, I should put them into a black Maraja [phoen] and drive them off to Sisak, to the prison there, because at the time there wasn't a prison in Sunja. There was a small prison up at the front-line, but there would be nobody to deal with them there or guard them there. So I carried out that order and I drove them to the detention centre. They were taken over by the police there. And three years later, the Military Court in Zagreb heard the case, and I was a witness there during those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Those three soldiers, did they have any assistants, legal assistants?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I came to the command to tell them that, and he saw them in such a way as calling up his personal lawyer in Zagreb, who then went to Sisak, to the Detention Unit there, to solve the issue and deal with the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And who is the "he"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: The "he" is General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a piece of information, and I'm going to ask you whether you know anything about that. Was any staged execution -- was an execution staged in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that he would have them executed, but at that point when this was going on, in front of the fire brigade a large number of locals gathered who were members of the units from Sunja, and members of the police force, and everyone was told what would happen if similar situations repeated themselves in Sunja. And, actually, things like that didn't happen anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You said that it was the civilian police stopping your soldiers at the barge and ferry and found these goods on them. Do you know when the military police arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: The military police arrived at the end of October, beginning of November, and Mr. Praljak brought them in, brought people in from outside whom we didn't know, because he assumed and knew that the locals wouldn't be able to lock up their own -- their neighbours, if such a situation were to arise, so he brought in people from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Were you witnesses of any -- witness to any of these reactions on the part of General Praljak, apart from this instance that you told about, about the theft of goods from houses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a witness when -- or, rather, I witnessed when two of the people who were ferrying people to and fro, from Sisak and Zagreb to Sunja, weapons and so on, they refused to carry out a very important order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that order was and describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was talk of launching a great action to link up the Komarevo-Kozibrod -- or, rather, Sunja, Hrvatska Kojstana [phoen], Dubica and those units, and the order could only come from Zagreb, in writing, through -- on the ferry. Now, as General Praljak insisted that the ferry stay overnight on the Sunja side so that if anybody was wounded, they could be transported, these two turned a deaf ear to calls to take somebody across. However -- well, as the person carrying the order rang up the command in Sunja and said that these two men were refusing to ferry him across, the general issued orders to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please. The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in order to assess your answers, we have something missing. You seem to be someone well educated, but I don't know what you did before you joined the Croatian Army. Did you go to a school, to university? If so, could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated from secondary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that before you arrived in the 2nd Guards Brigade, you were a member of the Special Police of the Croatian Army. What exactly is the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the name, "Special Police," police actually going about the usual kinds of duties; protecting the law courts in Sisak and some important locations, nothing with respect to any military action, because there wasn't any in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand better now. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You were saying -- you were saying that there were two men manning the ferry and that they were brought to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of noise and shouting, and the two were arguing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: The general and one of those two ferrymen or bargemen. One of the ferrymen started shouting at the general, and there was a lot of shoving and pushing, as I say in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And describe what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of kicking in the bum, butt kicking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know why the general reacted that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I knew, because if an operation were underway and we hadn't received orders, then the two units would have encountered an ambush and there would have been slaughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like the transcript to be corrected on page 36, line 24. I'm going to read what it says in the record. It says that there was a lot of kicking in the bum or butt.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was there a lot of kicking or were there several kicks?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You mentioned the military police. I'd like to ask you whether you had any knowledge of any action on General Praljak's part towards the policemen, towards members of the military police, if their conduct was not in keeping with the rules of conduct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those members of the military police, after a certain amount of time, started taking more and more responsibility into their hands. They settled accounts with the soldiers physically, and there was some dangerous situations where there could be shooting, too. However, the general stopped all this and sent that group of military policemen back to Zagreb, or Sisak, or wherever they had come from, and he set up a new military police platoon made up of locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So it wasn't a problem that these were locals anymore? He didn't have any problem with the locals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no more problems. Orders were no longer rejected. There were no more problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you is to tell us what was forbidden. What did General Praljak forbid when you were in Sunja, or have you already told us this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was forbidden to touch anybody's property. All the houses had been left vacant. And it was forbidden to shoot at somebody before that somebody shot at you. Then it was strictly forbidden to set fire to anything, and nothing was set fire to, in actual fact, down there. So all these measures and steps -- precautionary measures and steps were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if there was unnecessary shooting, what would the penalty be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the penalty and punishment depended on the units and the people involved, and they could be sent to do labour. You had to go and work at the bunkers and build the fortifications, for example. That was one of the assignments issued as a punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did they have to walk around?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to walk around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, tell us what you actually did.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was just a drill, a training. You had to walk just to keep your physique up. There were truces, and it was during a cease-fire that people fell casualty mostly because they were bored or things like that, so to prevent that he would make us go up to the front-line or, rather, below the front-line, which was called Zremen, the area, and we would have to walk two kilometres through a muddy field. And when we arrived, we saw a group of soldiers there who didn't even notice us, and we were ordered to put some masks on our heads and to make believe and simulate an attack, as if we were the enemy soldiers, because they hadn't noticed us coming at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And these were members of the HV, right, they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers standing guard up at the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on, then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: They were so taken up with their cooking - they were cooking something - that we managed to take them prisoner. This was simulation on our part. We sort of acted as if we were enemy soldiers and took them by surprise. So you can imagine what they felt like and how he punished them. I don't think they fared well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, was this leisurely behaviour the general type of behavior, like these people cooking and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't leave the front-lines, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about the guards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the lines lower down were secured by people who had bunkers in front of their own houses. They were people from the village who would just leave their bunkers during the day, and there was a field -- a three-kilometre field in front of them, and they thought that nothing could happen. And on one occasion, in the village of Zremen, the whole village left their post at the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We're not going to mention the names of villages, but just tell me, if you can remember, whether there was another situation similar to that with a person leaving the bunker and going home into their own house. I'm jogging your memory because I know you're excited, so I'm just trying to help you remember.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The man had left his post at the bunker, and we appeared. We came into his yard, the yard of his house. Following orders from General Praljak to return to his post, he refused to do so and said, Well, nobody was going to attack, anyway, and he had to go about his business. He was a farmer and had to do his farming. And at that point, Mr. Praljak told me to kill his cow. I knew that that wouldn't actually happen. I staged it, and the farmer jumped up, left everything he was doing, took up his rifle and went back to the bunker, and never again to leave his post at the bunker after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you talk to General Praljak and ask him why he said he wanted you to kill the man's cow?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's along the lines of what I was telling you earlier on. You had to take a strict stand with some people. He had to deal with them this way, and he just said, That's the peasant mentality for you. If you set fire to his house and to anything else, he's not going to be angry with you, but if you kill his cow, then watch out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You just said that everything was adapted to the situation and that he would adapt himself to the situation, that certain situations required certain actions. Now, when General Praljak physically punished somebody for some misdemeanor, was that not a sign that you could behave in similar fashion towards other people? When I say "you," I mean the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Why not? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, I mean if General Praljak hits the ferryman or does what he did with the cow, who's to say that this isn't sending a signal out to you that you could act in similar fashion, that you could beat someone up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course we couldn't do that because we knew the hierarchy very well. We knew who could do what at any given moment, so you couldn't walk along the road and settle accounts with anybody you felt like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you have any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, when you confirm that Praljak punished people physically, what do you have in mind, specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, take that ferryman, for instance. That -- the interpretation of "physical," well, the man wasn't beaten so badly that he would be in hospital for five days. He could go back to his job the very next day. So during that next day, a soldier was drowning and he jumped in and saved him. It was enough for him to show that he would act, if need be that he would settle accounts physically with people, but they weren't beaten up so badly that they ended up in hospital. So the second day, this same man saved the life of this other soldier on the ferry, and then he was commended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have heard that, and I was not suggesting that he -- that Praljak acted in an excessive way. But the examples you have given seem to be very impulsive. With the punishment I have in mind, I associate a situation where someone has done something wrong, he is told, You have done something wrong, and then comes the punishment, which if it is physical, can be formal, a certain amount of strokes, or can still be informal, a slap in the face. Can you say anything about that, or was your observation perhaps, what you said, not so technical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was involved in situations where an order was issued to a man on the front-line to do something or the other, and that person refused, stood up and started moving or wants to engage in a physical reaction -- in a physical action. So he would come in to react against those who did things against the war of law [as interpreted]. Such situations on the front-line existed. There was no military police, there was no police at all, and somebody had to do their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I have understood correctly, you said that General Praljak sometimes resorted to force to make sure that discipline was respected. I may have made a mistake, and I stand to be corrected. If I make a mistake, I'd be grateful if you corrected me. From what I understood, General Praljak sometimes kicked a soldier in the buttocks when he had misbehaved. Was this something you saw with your own eyes or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the case that I described involving the ferryman with my own two eyes. I eye-witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can understand, for instance, that a father slaps his child in the face, for instance, if his child has stolen sweets without parents' approval, but when it is a case of a military commander, who can demonstrate violence vis-a-vis one of his subordinates, don't you think this could have a negative impact on his soldiers, who will capture men and give this prisoner an order, Stand in line, and then the prisoner doesn't obey, and then the soldiers would hit the man in question? Do you think this could have an effect on his men or not? I understand that my question is a very tricky one. This is the case put by the Prosecution. This question has already been put by the Prosecution. Since you are an eye-witness, what I'm interested in is to know what your feelings about this were. Did you agree or did you disagree? You are the first person to actually mention this, so it's the right time to ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen. It was a message, one could say, to us as well. Just contrary to what you have said, we knew that we were not supposed to do any similar thing to any possible prisoner of war. We were made aware of that. But the soldier who was kicked in the butt, as you say, several times, if he had been reported to the Military Court, at best he could have ended in jail. In any case, I think that he fared much better the way he did. I must say that we are now talking about things that had to be put in the context of the times. It's very difficult for anybody who wasn't there, and who doesn't understand what was happening, to understand the whole context and the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a short question for you. The regulators enshrine in their codes whatever they wish to enshrine in any country. Now, as far as military rules are concerned, sometimes include corporal punishment. The question I'd like to put to you is this: I'd like to know, since you are a former major in the Croatian Army, as is General Praljak a former general in the Croatian Army, I wanted to know whether, in the military rules -- or let's say was it admitted that corporal punishment was acceptable? Was this part of the military rules in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does not exist in the rules of the Croatian Army. However, in 1991, 47 men and 100-plus civilians on the front-line were not the Croatian Army. Those were the beginnings of the creation of what would eventually turn into the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'll ask you once again, because now we have a whole picture. You've already told us, but repeat, please. Why was it important? Why did you just say that they could have ended up in jail, serving a long sentence? Why was it important for the message to reach the command? Was there any operation -- military operation that was under threat? Were the lives of soldiers and civilians under threat? Why was it so important for the message to reach the command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the lives of the soldiers and civilians alike were under threat, the lives of the soldiers of the two units with whom we were supposed to embark on an operation together, at the same time. Can you imagine what would have happened if such two units started and, because of a stupid omission, we did not receive any command? Can you imagine what the consequences would have been? I believe that the consequences would have surpassed any type of any punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We're talking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the name of the operation, because it was lost in the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The interpreter has asked me to repeat the name of the operation because we overlapped. I asked you whether we're still talking about the event involving the ferryman. Please wait and then answer. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the incidence that we are talking about. We are talking about the D-Day operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that involved the story with the ferryman, that Operation D-Day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We are privy to the information that I would like you to describe for the Trial Chamber about the incident when Radio 101 came to Sunja and when there were some playful soldiers, to put it that way. Could you describe, in your own words, what happened and what kind of punishment was involved in that situation, if there was, indeed, any punishment at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of September/October 1991, a group of young people from Zagreb arrived and established a radio service in Sunja so that people on the front-line could receive greetings from their loved ones. A girl was there. She also came with that group of people, and she brought a cat from Zagreb, that was her cat. Four members of the Croatian Army at the time were on their way back from Zagreb. They returned from Zagreb, went to the radio station, and wanted to order a few songs, and then she told them that they had to wait a little. One of the soldiers took the cat and threw her -- threw the cat against the radiator and killed the cat. The girl started crying, came to me. I conveyed all that to the general. At that very moment, the general appeared up there, disarmed all the four soldiers. He removed their insignia and their uniforms and sent them packing for Zagreb, and those men were never again members of the Croatian Army in Sunja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And how did you explain the whole thing to yourself? How did you interpret General Praljak's reaction to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a message, of course. The message was, If you can be removed from the Croatian Army on account of a cat, you should also be aware of what can happen to you on account of a human being.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: How was it with unnecessary shooting? And we've already spoken about that. What was the punishment for unnecessary shooting? Can you tell us why the 15th of January, 1992, is important for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: That is one of the most important dates in our history. That's the date when Croatia was recognised by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Where were you when Croatia was recognised by the international community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Sunja, on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was that recognition celebrated? And if it was, can you describe how?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV CRNKOVIC
